utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Could you please call the case, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for the day starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Morning Your Honours, good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Inger de Ru, April Carter, and Barney Thomas for the Prosecution this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Thomas. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning to all. Tina Drolec, Oonagh O'Connor, Novak Lukic, Gregor Guy-Smith and Boris Zorko on behalf of Mr. Perisic. And Mr. Zorko will be leading the witness this morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Our next witness is Mr. Radomir Gojovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration. May he please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir. And good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Gojovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: First of all, for the record, I'd like to ask you to give us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I am Radomir Gojovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: And your date and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 1st of February, 1943, in the village of Sekiraca, the Kursumlija municipality, the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: You are not appearing before this court for the first time. Can you tell us in what trials you testified and when?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I testified in the Slobodan Milosevic trial and in the Ojdanic et al trial, all the others incorporated in that indictment. And in the Djordjevic trial. I don't know what his first name is. Vlastimir Djordjevic, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, General, although you are not here for the first time, I am going to tell you of some rules we have to observe during the proceedings. And to be efficient in our work, so after my question and your answer -- or rather after my question, please pause before you give your answer and you can also look at how your words appear on the screen in front of you. General, briefly, I'm going to go through your curriculum vitae and you will confirm whether what I've read out is correct, once again for the record. You graduated from the gymnasium in Sarajevo and then the Faculty of Law in Sarajevo on the 28th of June, 1971; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: You did your internship at the military court with the military prosecutor and the Ministry of Justice in Sarajevo. After taking your bar exam you were the deputy prosecutor in Sarajevo from March 1973 until the 31st of October, 1976; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: From November 1976 up until the 12th of October, 1980, the investigating judge at the military court in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: From the 13th of October, 1980, to the end of 1984, you were the deputy military defender of the military disciplinary court of the command of the 7th Army; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: From the 1st of January, 1985, until June 1988 you were a judge, the president of the criminal chamber at the military court in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: From the 1st of July, 1988, until the end of 19 -- or rather, from the 1st of July, 1988, to the end of 1989 you were the deputy military prosecutor in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: In the meantime, you received your MA from the Faculty of Law in Belgrade in the chair for criminal law on the 2nd of November, 1989; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: From the 1st of January, 1990, you were the military prosecutor in Sarajevo until the end of June 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: From the 1st of July, 1992, until the 31st of December, 1993, you were the deputy supreme military prosecutor in Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: From the 1st of January, 1994, until the 16th of April, 1999, you were the president of the military court in Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: From the 16th of April, 1990, until the 31st of March, 2001, you were the chief of the legal administration in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia in the Ministry of Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: April 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to say in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia first and then in the Ministry of Defence because those were two different institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Your professional military service ceased on the 1st of April, 2001 when you reached mandatory retirement conditions?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Therefore, General, in addition to your troop service in the military education and training which lasted for ten years in the legal service, first of all in the Yugoslav People's Army and then in the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, you performed all the functions that were required over a 30-year period; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from that review you can see my professional development in the legal military organs, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, in addition to these professional duties that you had, did you have any other functions in the course of your career?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. After I had retired in the General Staff in the Ministry of Defence of the Army of Yugoslavia, a commission was established for co-operation with the International Criminal Tribunal here in The Hague, and I was elected to be the deputy president of the commission. I accepted that post, so I was the only pensioner, or rather, there were two of us, two of us were retired, all the rest were professional officers from the General Staff and the Ministry of Defence in that commission and the commission numbered some ten member, some eight members.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, General. Now, General, can you briefly explain to us what in the SFRY, and later on in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the military justice office represented? What did the judiciary represent in the sense of its work, its responsibilities and so on?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Based on the law governing military courts in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and later on in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, military courts were independent and autonomous institutions in the system of justice and jurisdiction in the country in addition to the other regular civilian courts. And they were in charge of trying members of the Army of Yugoslavia, or rather the Army of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and certain other individuals outside the army for specific crimes under the law governing military courts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, in view of the crisis that existed in the beginning of the 1990s in the SFRY, can you explain to us what happened to the existing military judiciary with respect to the crises and its development and the ultimate dissolution of the state?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: With the escalation of the crisis in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, we saw a violent cessation by certain units, republics; first of all this occurred in Slovenia, and when the decision was taken for the units of the Yugoslav People's Army to withdraw from that territory, this held true for the military courts and military prosecutors too, so the military court and military prosecuted in Ljubljana, because the seat was in Ljubljana, the capital of Slovenia, ceased to function and this later on was mirrored and happened in Croatia so that the military court in Croatia, in Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, we are trying to type what you are saying and you are talking too fast. You are leaving the typist behind. Could you please just slow down so that we are able to keep pace with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. I apologise. Let me repeat what I just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the violent cessation of Slovenia when the decision was made at the level of the SFRY for the units of the Yugoslav People's Army to withdraw from the territory of Slovenia, the work of the military court ceased and it had its seat up until then in Ljubljana. Furthermore, when the situation in Croatia escalated and when the units of the JNA withdrew from the territory of the Republic of Croatia, the military court and military prosecutor's office ceased functioning in Zagreb, and the military court and military prosecutor's office for the navy, the seat of which was in Split, with a part of the judges and some of the prosecutors, was relocated to the Republic of Montenegro to a small place called Tivat on the shores of the Adriatic coast. And that is where they continued to work under the new conditions. In 1992, the situation escalated in Bosnia and Herzegovina so that the same thing happened, and from that republic the units of the JNA were withdrawn from the territory, and the military court and military prosecutor ceased functioning in Sarajevo at the end of May 1992. And after that from the military prosecutor's office in Sarajevo I moved to Belgrade. After that the military court under these conditions re-organised themselves, so to speak, and the military court and the military prosecutor's office continued to operate in Belgrade, as well as those in Tivat and the military and the military prosecutor's office in Nis. So they operated on the territorial principle. Later on, the military court moved from Tivat to Podgorica where a military court was set up there that took over the jurisdiction of the military court from Tivat for the territory of Montenegro and part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have in e-court document of the Prosecution P1187, and at the same time I would kindly ask the usher to give the binder to the witness. Of course it should first be shown to the Prosecution so that we can continue to work smoothly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, the document that we see on our screens is marked with tab 2 in your binder. That's where you can find it. General, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: This is the Law on Military Courts published in the "Official Gazette" of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you. Please focus your attention on Article 2 which reads that the military courts in executing their judicial function shall be independent and autonomous. Can you please explain in more detail what this independence and autonomous status of military courts means?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: It is very well known in theory that there are three branches in any state, i.e., the executive branch, the judiciary, and the executive. They are all independent from one another. Military courts in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were completely independent from the two remaining branches of government because one of the two branches can have any influence on the third branch, which is to say judiciary. So this, in short, meant that the courts were independent. As far as autonomous work of the court refers to -- that refers to the judges which means that they carry out their duties completely independently and they operate according to their discretion. They do not render judgements under anyone's influence or suggestion or proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you please look now at Article 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's page 3 in B/C/S and page 15 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, can you see that article?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: I'm not going to read the text of this article. I would like to ask you about the permanence of tenure?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what is provided here under Article 22 when it comes to the position of a judge. Once a judge is appointed to this post, that is an indefinite appointment which is not limited in time and that is the factor that guarantees his independence by providing him with security in his post. And it can be fulfilled only under the conditions as provided under this law. Unlike some other solutions where judges were appointed to a four-year tenure and were entitled to be re-elected, here we have a different situation which was very progressive and modern one, which granted the Judges a permanent tenure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Tell us, who is it who appoints the military judges to their functions?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The military judges and military prosecutors are appointed by the president of the republic by his decree based on the detailed proposal, later called detailed opinion, provided by the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, let us be quite clear. When we are talking about the appointment of judges now, we are talking about the situation in the FRY; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. General, in Articles 9 and 10 there is mention of jurisdiction of the military courts. With regard to which criminal offences do we have the jurisdiction afforded to military courts?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: According to Article 9 of the Law on Military Courts, the military courts try military personnel for all criminal offences committed by them. These criminal offences are listed in the Criminal Code. In addition to that, the military courts conduct trials against other individuals as well. These other individuals include civilians or non-military personnel but for very specific criminal offences, and these specific criminal offences are also included in the Law on Military Courts by granting jurisdiction to the military courts to try such individuals for such offences. And it also tries civilians serving or working in the army for the offences relating to their service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 2 in B/C/S and page 5 in English where we have the aforementioned articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, does this jurisdiction include conducting trials by military courts in the FRY with respect to the criminal offences against humanity and international criminal law?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if it involves military personnel, so all the crimes, criminal acts, provided by the criminal law including the acts against the international criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: You said against military personnel, didn't you? There's probably some distinction there, can you tell us what was the case with civilians, under whose jurisdiction did they fall?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking about criminal offences against international criminal law, if they are committed by another individual then a civilian court has jurisdiction, not a military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: There were also civilian prosecutors in the judiciary of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, because without a prosecutor, no court can operate. There is an interface between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you. General, if a criminal act is committed by a number of co-perpetrators but only a few of them are military personnel, who has the jurisdiction in such cases, a military court or a civilian court?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Article 12 provides that if members of the military and the civilians commit a criminal act jointly, but this is not a crime that falls under the jurisdiction of the military court, then, in that instance, the court that has jurisdiction of the civilian individual has jurisdiction of the military personnel as well. So in that case it means a civilian court will try a member of the military who committed a crime together with a civilian, provided they did not commit a criminal act that is enshrined in the Law on the Military courts that we mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one correction in the transcript, line 14 -- no, line 15, page 12, it should say exclusive jurisdiction. That's now all right. Thank you for this correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, did the law speak about command responsibility in the period that we are discussing as one of the forms of liabilities?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: In the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and later on in the criminal judiciary system of the FRY, there is no command responsibility provided as liability with respect to committing a criminal offence, including offences against international criminal law. There is only -- there's not only direct intent, but a qualified intent which means that there should be a clear intent to commit a certain crime. So the only form of liability is direct intent with additional intention to commit a crime. Other than that, there was no mention of the so-called command responsibility which is based on objective responsibility. It would mean that it would suffice that if you have a commanding officer and someone commits a crime, the commanding officer should have known or would have known about this felony and thereby should be held responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Speaking about criminal prosecution in the FRY, can you tell us whether there were any priorities set out with regard to criminal prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, in the work of military prosecutors and prosecutors in general who are authorised to prosecute individuals for criminal acts, it goes without saying that his priorities would be to prosecute the perpetrators who committed the most serious crimes. The same applies to the courts. That's the principle of how these institutions operate. These cases are given priority because they carry a much more serious social peril and produce more serious consequences, and therefore, they are given priority compared to some lesser crimes or ordinary criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Speaking about the status of a military personnel, do the military courts have jurisdiction, as well as the Prosecutors, with regard to conducting proceedings against such individuals for acts committed during their professional service, or is there any change under such circumstances with regard to jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Awhile ago we spoke about the overall jurisdiction of military courts to try military personnel, so for as long as one is a member of the military, the law provides precisely who is afforded the status of a member of the military. First of all, these are professional soldiers commissioned and non-commissioned officers, conscripts, reservists, et cetera. In life it often happens that someone's status of that nature ceases to exist within this period. For example, an officer whose active-duty service is terminated is no longer a member of the military. Under some circumstances if a criminal proceedings are instituted, after the suspension of the status, the jurisdiction of the continued prosecution comes into question. In such situations, if this does not involve criminal acts or other criminal offences that are specifically under the jurisdiction of military courts, the military courts will relinquish their jurisdiction and will no longer act against such individuals provided the indictment has become legally valid. If that was the case, it was the military courts who are obliged to bring the proceedings to the end. If we are talking about the stage of investigation or pre-trial proceedings, the military courts cannot try such individuals and these cases are deferred to civilian prosecutors and civilian courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you explain to us, with respect to proceedings, what it means when an indictment becomes fully valid, comes into force or legally valid?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Once the prosecutor raises an indictment and presents it to the court, there is a phase during which the indictment is re-examined by the court. During that stage of re-examination, that is to say the judge who receives the case first of all checks to see whether the indictment was raised by the competent prosecutor, whether it fulfills all the legal conditions and elements stipulated for an indictment, and whether it is a crime which is provided for in the indictment for which the prosecutor states his views. Now, if all these formal conditions have been met, the president of the chamber verifies to see whether the court is still responsible or not, whether it has jurisdiction to see whether the individual has -- is no longer an employee of the army. Now, if that is not the case, then the indictment is sent to the accused and to his defence counsel, and they then have the right to lodge an appeal and challenge the validity of the indictment, the legality of the indictment, and anything else that it can use to challenge the indictment. Now, once the appeal is received, then a trial chamber made up of three judges decide and rule on the appeal, and if they reject the appeal as unfounded, or if there was no appeal and a time-limit of eight days has expired in which an appeal is to be lodged, then the indictment comes into force legally. And analogously in this tribunal it's confirmed by a judge, but here it is confirmed by the three judges, if an appeal was lodged, if not, by force of law, it comes into force, it can be acted upon, a trial can be scheduled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now going to move on to another area, or rather, we will go back to document P1187, which is a Prosecution exhibit still on our screens, but can we look at page 7, please, in B/C/S, and page 34 in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: And, General, I'd like to focus your attention on Article 74. General, this Article 74 deals with the organisation and work of military courts during a state of war, and I'd like to hear your comments, or rather, further explanation of what is stated in this article.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: This provision of the law regulates the organisation and work of the military courts during war. Once a state of war is proclaimed, an emergency situation comes into force in which it is necessary to organise the work of military courts differently to peacetime, that is to say adjusted to the newly-arisen situation in a state of war. This provides for the possibility and direct responsibility of having peacetime military courts, which, in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, there were three, cease to function. The supreme military court and supreme military prosecutor in working with the staff of the Supreme Command and courts are established attached to the commands of individual units and there are many more of them. So military courts are set up attached to the commands of the military districts, so these are territorial military organs in a certain area attached to the commands of the corps, divisions, and armies, command of the air force and anti-air attacks and the navy. So all these units have new courts attached to their commands and parallel to that we have military prosecutors, they follow suit. So they continue their work under the new conditions and there are many more of them. The object being that they should be closer and become part of the units involved where they have the conditions of working more efficaciously and prosecuting the perpetrators of crimes more efficiently, the members of those units, to try only the members of those units. And the same applies to the supreme military court and military prosecutor. They set up their departments, the supreme military court and supreme military prosecutor sets up their departments attached to the commands of the armies so that they are in a position to function effectively and to deal with appeals lodged with first-instance courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The military judiciary organs of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, after the dissolution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, did they work in peacetime conditions or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The military courts in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, after the disintegration of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, were organised and worked in peacetime conditions. They functioned right up until the proclamation of a state of war when there was the NATO pact aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the 24th of March, 1999. And this organisation and war time establishment functioned only while there was a state of war. Once the state of war ceases, their organisational and work on those principles ceases as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have pulled up on e-court Exhibit P1188.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, in your binder it is tab 3. It is the law governing military prosecutors. General, before we move on to another area, you said here that the courts, the military courts in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia functioned in conformity with Article 74 of the 24th of March, 1999. Can you just tell us up until what date did that state exist, situation exist?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: That was during the state of war, and as far as I remember, the state of war ceased on the 24th of June or 25th of June, 1999, one of those two days. I'm not quite sure whether it was the 20th of June or the 25th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you. General, take look at the Law on Military Prosecutors and Article 1 in particular in which it states that: "The military prosecutor is an independent state organ ...," so could you explain to us the meaning of the concept of independence and autonomy?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Analogous to the independence and autonomous of the courts and the process of decision-making, so also the military prosecutor and prosecutors in general are independent and autonomous state organs which prosecute the perpetrators of crimes. So the prosecutor is completely independent in making his decisions with respect to criminal prosecution. It is the sole organ that has that responsibility and therefore it is quite normal and natural that the prosecutor be independent and autonomous in making his decisions, which, of course, have to conform to the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd also like us, General, to look at Article 28 of this same law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So may we have that displayed on e-court, please. Page 3 of the B/C/S and 11 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, it says here that the tenure of the military prosecutor and his deputies shall be permanent. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: That means just as applied to judges, that the function of the prosecutor and his deputies once appointed to the post is permanent, which is once again a guarantee of security for the post and the person forming that function, that is to say that they are able to make their decisions completely independently and autonomously and that they can rest assured that that is the condition on which they will perform their function; that is to say that nobody can replace them outside the conditions provided for by the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Tell us, please, who appoints military prosecutors to that duty?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Military prosecutors and deputy military prosecutors, just like judges, are appointed by the president of the republic, and there is a statement of reasons that needs to accompany the appointment, so a statement of reasons by the minister of defence. With your permission, I'd like to explain how this functioned in practice. There is a legal decision whereby the minister of defence makes a proposal and expounds his reasons, but in practice, as far as judges are concerned and prosecutors and deputy prosecutors, that opinion is compiled by the military prosecutors or presidents of the courts for potential candidates. And in 99 per cent of the cases, if the members of the court and president of the court propose somebody after holding consultations then that person is appointed, the candidate is appointed because there is no other institution within the army which has such close knowledge about the qualities of a candidate as do colleagues amongst themselves. So the minister of defence is not the -- somebody who just takes out a file from his drawer and proposes somebody, but he takes on board opinions given by the candidate's colleague so that it wasn't a unilateral act, it required broad consultation for putting forward and appointing the candidate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, briefly could you describe for us the responsibilities that the military prosecutor had in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The military prosecutor, in simple terms, is in charge of prosecuting the perpetrators of crimes which come under the remit of the military court, so the affairs of the military court are affairs that the military prosecutor deals with outside that scope not, so they are mutually correlated. If somebody raises an indictment against an individual who does not fall within that category, then the indictment will be rejected and they cannot take the proceedings any further under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have called up on e-court page 2 of the B/C/S and 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: And, General, I'd like to ask you to take a look at Article 9. And in this article it states that the military prosecutor shall take action within the bounds of his subject matter and territorial jurisdiction. Can you help us to understand those two concepts, subject matter and territorial jurisdiction, what does that actually mean?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Subject matter means that the prosecutor or the military court must act within the frameworks of its remit, that is to prosecute the perpetrators of crimes for which it is responsible. That is to say it is their responsibility to prosecute all military personnel committing a crime, so military personnel, any crimes committed and others for crimes which under the law they can prosecute. Now, the territorial jurisdiction is linked to territory, crimes and perpetrators on territories over which he has actual responsibility. And that territory is determined by the law governing military courts in the corresponding article which enumerates --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, I apologise but I think you are moving a bit too fast. Could you slow down.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The territory over which a specific court has jurisdiction is identical to the one that has the prosecutor, so we are talking about territorial jurisdiction which is also provided by the Law on Military Courts which specifies municipalities as basic units of state organisation. Each municipality has its territory and its boundaries. In some places, military units and military institutions or installations are located, and if a crime is committed in that specific territory that falls under the subject matter jurisdiction of the prosecutor, then he will prosecute. So territorial jurisdiction is relating to specific territory and subject matter is a general concept which means that he is entitled to prosecute. That practically means that neither the court nor the prosecutor can act outside the boundaries of their jurisdictions. They can only do that if a case is delegated to them by the supreme military prosecutor, and in case of courts if that is done by the supreme military court, but that is done only for practical purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, can you please repeat the last sentence because I'm not sure whether it's been recorded correctly with regard to jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Territorial jurisdiction implies that a military prosecutor or a military court are entitled to act with regard to criminal offences committed in the territory that they have jurisdiction over in geographical terms. And that is regulated by the Law on Military Courts. Exceptionally, it can happen that they act outside those boundaries, territorial boundaries set out by the law, if a case is being deferred to their jurisdiction that does not coincide with their territorial jurisdiction. The proposal is made by the military prosecutor, supreme military prosecutor, and in case of courts it can be done by the supreme military court. So if we are talking about prosecution, it has to be delegated by the prosecutor and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness please slow down. These are very complicated and complex matters. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Gojovic, can you please slow down once again. I know that once we get into the subject matter we sort of forget about other things happening and we move a little faster. Can we please slow down. The interpreters can't keep up with you. Yes, Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, you started your sentence referring to the prosecutor's office, you said that the case is referred to by, can you finish it.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: If the act is under the territorial jurisdiction of the prosecutor in Belgrade, for example, and for practical and tactical reasons these proceedings can more easily be done by the prosecutor in Nis, then the Belgrade prosecutor will defer the case to Nis and he will also ask the military court to do the same and defer the case to the military court in Nis. Then the Supreme Court will pass a decision to that effect and will pass jurisdiction to the military court in Nis. Though that is as far as territorial jurisdiction is concerned. But in principle, each of those has responsibility for their specific territory but they can exceptionally try cases that are deferred to them from other territories. This same applies to civilian courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, General. Concerning professional responsibility, in what way was the system of military prosecutor's office organised, to whom were the prosecutors responsible for their work?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Military prosecutor and prosecutors in general within the judicial system of the FRY, the governing principle is the one of subordination. The first-instance prosecutor is duty-bound to act according to instructions and directions of his superior prosecutor. In other words, the first-instance military prosecutor is responsible for his work to the supreme military prosecutor, whereas the supreme military prosecutor is responsible for first-instance prosecutor's work and for his own work as well to the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you please look again at Exhibit P1188, Article 6, sub-item 1. In this article it is stipulated that the right and the duty of a military prosecutor is to prosecute perpetrators of criminal acts including, but not limited to, to undertake measures with regard to discovering crimes and -- detecting crimes and discovering their perpetrators. Can you please give us a more detailed explanation about the process of taking these measures and what these measures actually involve according to the law?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Proceeding from his basic function and jurisdiction of each prosecutor and including a military prosecutor which is to prosecute perpetrators of specific crimes, in carrying out his duties, there is no problem if the perpetrator's identity is known and if the specific crime has been detected. Under such circumstances, all the organs who are in charge of conducting their duties at these initial stages will do so. And of course, a prerequisite is for the crime to have been reported. The problem that a prosecutor faces and the law enforcement becomes prominent if the identity of the perpetrator is unknown or if it is known that a criminal act has been committed but there is no solid evidence or even circumstantial or initial evidence to that effect and it is obvious that a criminal offence is such that should be prosecuted ex officio by the prosecutor because there are some minor offences that can be regulated through a civil suit. Under such circumstances, the prosecutor has at his disposal, as it is worded here, a mechanism of undertaking measures, which is rather general. It is not specified which measures this particularly involves. I agree with that. However, if you look at other legal provisions not only from the Law on Military Prosecutor and the Military Courts, but other laws as well from which these measures can be identified, this would mean that the prosecutor is entitled to ask certain state organs, which is primarily the investigating and detecting organs which exist in the army and in society in general. In civilian life, that is the organs of the interior, i.e., the police and the army, this is military police, security organs, command organs, officers, institutions, work organisations and other entities. So from all these entities that might provide relevant facts or information, the prosecutor is authorised to seek this information. On the other hand, all these organs are also obliged to act pursuant to his request and to provide the information or the facts or the documents that they have and that they possess. So this is a whole array of measures that the prosecutor can undertake within the scope of his own responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, I will interrupt you for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this is a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm trying to find out where we are going with all this. I thought we --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will soon complete this topic which had to do with the jurisdiction held by various bodies in terms of detecting and prosecuting crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, we left off when we were dealing with the responsibility of the prosecutor and the measures taken by him. In what way does the prosecutor gather information about a crime?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago I described the way which he tried to obtain information from relevant state bodies. In any state where there is a rule of law, and I think that the FRY and even earlier on was a state with a legal system. The prosecutor would apply to the specialised bodies dealing with the detection and prevention of crime to gather information as well as to any other stated body or agency which would come across relevant information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. On the issue of information gathering, can you tell us who has the responsibility to establish that the information gathered is of such a nature as to require prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: This is both the right and the obligation of the prosecutor having jurisdiction. The prosecutor is the one who undertakes prosecution, other bodies are not vested with this right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Specifically when it comes to the Army of Yugoslavia, did every commanding officer, senior officer, have an obligation to take certain measures where he learns that a criminal act has been committed by members of his unit and which measures are these?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Any senior or commanding officer, regardless of the level or the unit he commands, where it so happens that a member of his unit has committed a crime for which prosecution is initiated ex officio has certain obligations to meet, specifically he or she needs to take measures to make sure that the perpetrator of a crime where he is identified should be taken into custody to prevent him from absconding. In other words, the commanding officer is even entitled to take him into custody to detain him, or otherwise to take measures that will ensure that the perpetrator doesn't flee. As for the crime itself, the officer needs to take measures to secure the scene of crime which means that only on-site investigation officers can have access to the crime scene. He needs to make sure that trace evidence and evidence is preserved and she needs to take steps to gather additional information that may shed light on this event. Finally, he also needs to provide all the up-to-date information to the prosecutor having jurisdiction, and where this isn't possible, to report to the immediately superior command that will in turn inform the prosecution having jurisdiction and the law enforcement organs who will take it up from there and see to their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you. General, the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, what were it's relations with the military prosecutor's offices and military courts?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: According to the earlier Law on Military Courts and Military Prosecutor's Office when say I earlier, I mean the one preceding the one we discussed, since the military prosecutors were supposed to serve the commands of the armies, whereas the main administration of the General Staff dealt with the status-related records of those who were employed in the military judiciary. A functional relationship between the military courts and military prosecutor's offices on the one hand and the General Staff on the other hand did not exist because the military judiciary acted independently. Thus, not only did they not have a functional relationship with the General Staff, but they also didn't have any with the administrations except for the part where they dealt with procurement from the technical administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just add that once the 1995 law was carried, not even procurement was in the hands of the General Staff. Rather, it was in the hands of the Ministry of Defence which meant that the military judiciary bodies relied for procurement on the logistics bodies of the Ministry of Defence, so even this link with the General Staff concerning procurement was severed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: You are talking about procurement or supplies. Can you tell us what sort of supplies these were?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: In order for the courts and prosecutor's offices as a unit to operate, they needed stationery, office equipment, vehicles, and of course salaries as well. All these technical matters were within the responsibility of other bodies to deal with for the benefit of the military judiciary which did not have its own departments dealing with this because it would not have been reasonable for them to have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, did the Chief of the General Staff in the period before the establishment of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and thereafter have the right to initiate -- to launch an investigation to be conducted on the part of the prosecutor? And if so, under which conditions?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: When it came to crimes for which prosecutors and military prosecutors initiated investigation ex officio, the prosecutor will first of all receive notice of crime, that's to say, the criminal report from police, military police, security, inspection, control, et cetera. Only rarely would they receive notice of it from superior officers, rather they would come from these bodies. When it comes to the Chief of the General Staff, which is the highest-ranking position within an army, it was not within his purview to file criminal reports. It fell upon the lower levels to do so. Generally speaking, under the law and the constitution of a state, every citizen has the obligation to report a crime. And in addition to this civic obligation, the Chief of the General Staff did not have any additional powers vested with him. They were not ruled out absolutely, but that they would deal in that case with some other issues, whereas crime fell within the purview of specialised bodies and departments which normally exist within an army for that particular purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would like to move to a different topic now. As far as the provisions of international law are concerned, did the FRY have a system to implement these provisions, and I mean did it have a legal order to that effect?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, pursuant to its constitution from 1992, I believe, Article 16 para 2, provided for all treaties which were ratified in keeping with the constitution and other internationally-recognised norms, and made them a component part of the country's legal order. From that followed that all the Geneva Conventions and other treaties which the SFRY had ratified and which were accepted by the FRY, made part and parcel of the legal order of the country. This included all the conventions relating to International Humanitarian Law. Additionally, in addition to the constitution there was the Criminal Code which provided for the crimes punishable under international law and these crimes incurred the maximum sentence envisaged under the FRY legal system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You mentioned the constitution just now. Were there any other legal instruments in the FRY which provided for these very issues?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the constitution, the Law on Defence included a provision whereby any member of the Army of Yugoslavia in the course of combat was duty-bound to adhere to all the rules of -- and laws of war in treating the wounded, the prisoners, and civilians. This was binding on all the members of the Army of Yugoslavia engaged in combat. In addition to that, the Law on Defence envisaged that members of the army should employ their weapons in combat in accordance with the rules governing the use of weapons, and this of course relates to their use of fire-power against the enemy forces in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In addition to what you've just stated, did the Army of Yugoslavia, including the General Staff, take any measures to make sure that the provisions of International Humanitarian Law were complied with by members of the army?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: In the military schools and academies, among other subjects and courses, there was one which dealt with the application of provisions of International Humanitarian Law. All those attending these schools would hear this course and had to sit the exam on this course and this was a system of educating them on this matter, among others. I know that in the course of 1995, based on a protocol signed between the Ministry of Defence and the ICRC, certain seminars were organised for members of the VJ at the level of the General Staff where ICRC instructors held seminars for senior officers at certain levels who in turn would train their subordinates. It was a train-the-trainers course which lasted over just more than two years. These were sets of seminars and training on the provisions of International Humanitarian Law based on the protocol I referred to. I know of this because at the time I was a lecturer at the military academy on the issue of criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Please turn to your binder, tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we call up in e-court document 01315D. This is a 65 ter Defence document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: We have the document on our screens. Do you recognise the document, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the document. These are rules of conduct in combat produced by the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, specifically its first administration. This was updated and consolidated material and it was known to be part of combat gear of every soldier, and he would be given this along with the other gear at the time of his mobilisation in times of war or imminent threat of war. Every soldier would be given this brochure that was printed on waterproof paper and the soldier would be given this brochure along with the other kit that he would be given. The brochure related in the briefest of terms, the rules of engagement and the soldier would always have it to hand, and would also have to familiarise himself with it under the supervision of his superior officer. We had a similar brochure earlier on when every unit, whenever mobilisation plans would be drawn up, would make sure that its soldiers received this brochure. It's just that this issue was a bit updated and embellished, so to speak. But it was a standard part of every soldier's kit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document into evidence now, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The only comment I'd make, Your Honour -- I am sorry, Your Honours. The only comment I would make, Your Honours, is at this point we haven't had evidence on when this was in effect, during what period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, the document we saw a moment ago, during what period was it enforced? When was it applied? What period of time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously the Prosecutor wasn't following what I said, so I'll try and explain. This is nothing new. It's nothing new. It's just a brief summary taken from the 1949 Geneva Conventions and additional protocols, dated to 1970, and their short summaries and that is as part and parcel of every soldiers kit. And that was true for the 1960s onwards. And these specific ones in the material since this specific authentic document, this one was compiled after the seminars that were held that I mentioned earlier on by the international ICRC committee in 1995, 1996, 1997. So that's when this text was adapted and put down on this plastified [as interpreted] paper, waterproof paper. Previously they didn't have this plastic form but they were nevertheless part and parcel of the kit of every soldier. I know that from my own experience in the 1960s and 1970s. I had that as part of my kit when we were shown where our equipment was if war should break out. So this was stored -- the war reserves were stored in the central depot and this was part of the kit. This particular document dates to 1996 when it was compiled and the text adapted in the technical sense actually, this plastic version, but otherwise it always existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Now, you say what existed in the 1960s was always there, which would mean that what you had in the 1960s would not have had the -- in it the additional protocols which came after 1960. You are saying this particular one on the screen that we are looking at came about around 1995, 1996, 1997, you've given us those three dates after the International Committee of the Red Crosses meetings. Are we to understand then that this document here was not there during the war, 1992 to 1995, and that also the one before it which you had from the 1960s didn't have the 1979 protocol? So, in fact, we don't have before us anything that was in place during 1990 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll explain this once again. The document with these contents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your explanation I understood, sir. I understand the contents, yes. However, in 1960, the 1979 additional protocols were not there and you say you had them all the time going on, and then after the 1995, 1996, 1997 seminars, you had these, which now include the protocols. But these only came into effect within the FRY, as I say you gave us three dates, 1995, 1996, 1997. I'm saying to you, based on that explanation of yours, are we to understand that the document before us was non-existent in this the period 1990 to 1995? Please don't go back to explain what you explained. I understood you perfectly well. Just answer my question. The document before us was not there during 1990 to 1995? You can say yes, you can say no, you can say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President, but I'm not sure you understood me. With the adoption of the additional protocols, they were incorporated into a similar document which existed and was prepared for each and every soldier within its war reserve kit. This specific plastic version on plasticified paper was compiled, let's say in 1997, so it was plasticified in 1997. But the contents existed before that, it existed in 1992 and 1993, but in a different form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can I repeat my question. Not withstanding what I have just said, are we to understand that this plasticised form was non-existent in the period 1990 to 1995 because this plasticised form came in 1997 now that you have zoned it into one year? So the document you are seeing here is not the document which gave us the contents that were there between 1990 and 1995? They may have been there but this was not it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be closer to the microphones, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He hasn't started speaking yet, but can you get closer to the microphone, please, because the interpreters can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this particular form, so this specific document dates to 1997. Let's choose 1997, say 1997, and that's not being challenged. In this form and this edition and we can see that it's the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. Before that they were similar, with similar contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I think I've asked my question. Mr. Thomas, you had objected. Do you persist in your objection?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The answers have taken care of my objection, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may proceed, Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will stand by my proposal to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Yes, it is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D422. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, let's move and to another area. I would like you to explain to us what military discipline entails and means.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: That subject is regulated by rules and provisions, the law governing military discipline, first and foremost, and I'll try and interpret it, what the regulations are. When we say military discipline, we mean exact full and timely execution of military duties and other duties in the Army of Yugoslavia, in keeping with existing rules of service and other generally accepted norms and moral norms too. So that would in a nutshell be what military discipline means.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Are there violations of military discipline, and in what way do the norms regulate violations of military discipline?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The law governing the Army of Yugoslavia and laws governing military discipline regulate this in normative terms, what is implied under violation of military discipline, that is defined under those laws. And those norms provide for two types of infraction or violation which are legally qualified as breaches of military discipline, disciplinary mistakes or disciplinary infractions, violations. Disciplinary mistakes are less serious infractions of military discipline, a minor offence, and disciplinary violations are major offences against the laws governing military discipline. So we have minor and major violations, or offences. And any major offences are qualified under the law as crimes and so the meritorious decision is made by the prosecutor or court responsible when this has become -- when it's a major offence and constitutes the comitance of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: You mentioned in your answer a criminal offence. You mentioned that term. Now, if an act which is perpetrated comes under the heading of disciplinary responsibility and criminal responsibility or liability, was it possible, according to the provisions in place, to conduct a parallel proceedings against an individual, disciplinary and criminal proceedings for the perpetrator of that kind of offence?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: We have two situations there and I'll answer your direct question first. As an exception for the same acts committed of the perpetrator if he violates military discipline, if in committing those acts both a criminal act was committed and -- well, for the same act committed, a criminal proceedings can be undertaken by the prosecutor or the court and the responsible organ in the army, the military authority can also consider the act as being a disciplinary offence and then pass a sentence for disciplinary offences independently of the criminal proceedings launched. That's an exception of the rule. And that exception is to be invoked only if specific military interests demand that such proceedings be taken. Now, what do we mean by specific military interests? That is evaluated from one case to the other depending on the concrete situation and that evaluation and assessment is made by the superior officer in charge of those particular proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were talking about the exception to the rule. You also mentioned specific military interests, interests of the service. In what way does the superior officer in charge of unleashing proceedings determine when specific or special interests are involved for a particular member of the Army of Yugoslavia to be prosecuted for infraction of discipline?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Since it is a matter that the superior officer has to judge and assess, and the conclusion he reaches must serve a practical purpose, determining that it is really in the interests of the military service as such, so specific special interests involved, an understandable explanation may be given about what this looked like -- looks like in practice. A practical example is in order here. Mostly the superior officers, although these were exceptions and having worked in the army for many years, I know that they were indeed exceptions, it occurred very rarely, but anyway, the superior officers had to decide. The superior officer consults the prosecutor who under takes prosecution proceedings and if in consultations with him he deems it necessary that in the criminal proceedings, or rather, if he feels that the court cannot be expected to pass a sentence over two years imprisonment but below the two-year threshold and if a sentence of more than two years is expected, then if it is meted out on a army employee, on a soldier, then he is released from service. Now, if a judgement of that kind is not expected and it is deemed that the person committing the offence should no longer be a member of the army, then disciplinary proceedings are undertaken for disciplinary offences, and one of the sentences open to the military disciplinary court is the termination of service or stripping a soldier of his rank. So those then are the cases which would lead the superior officer to decide to conduct parallel proceedings. So if in the criminal proceedings a major offence has been committed and that it is obvious that a greater sentence would be given, then it's counter-productive to conduct disciplinary proceedings for disciplinary offences because the person would be dismissed from the army anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Just one thing to see if this has been recorded properly. You said if that was purposeful?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: No, I said that wouldn't serve any purpose. That would be counter-productive, that's what I said. That would involve work that would be futile and without any ultimate effect because the objective can be achieved in a more appropriate manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, if I understand you properly, you said that the objective is going to be achieved in a different manner. Tell me this: Is there any primacy or precedence when we talk about two types of proceedings to establish somebody's liability, that is to say either the disciplinary or criminal liability?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The prosecutor initiates proceedings within his purview completely independently, and there is no question of his relinquishing this to be dealt with in disciplinary procedure if the crime was serious. That would be anachronous and that would be contrary to the law. So he can't do that in any way. It is now up to the officer to decide whether he will leave this up to the prosecutor to decide and where the prospect of a higher sentence is evident, there is no need to launch disciplinary proceedings for such acts that would qualify him as a dishonourable member of the army. So this refers to only particular criminal offences, not all of them, and in that particular case, precedence is given to criminal proceedings irrespective of the fact that the officer thinks that the person involved deserves to be discharged from service, but on the other hand one cannot expect that he would be punished properly through criminal proceedings and he would go on with this process. This may happen for some minor offences when no criminal proceedings are launched at all which are of lesser importance and which would be conducive to the prosecutor rejecting the charges. It depends on the decision of the military court. The officer initiating the proceedings cannot be sure what the outcome and what the decision of the court would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, what happens with disciplinary responsibility in the event of a VJ member's service being terminated? I'm talking about jurisdiction for conducting disciplinary proceedings. Are we talking about the same organs or is there any shift in the jurisdiction? I am sorry. First of all, tell us who are the competent organs to initiate disciplinary proceedings before you answer my question?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The decision to launch disciplinary investigation about disciplinary violation is taken by an officer of the rank of the regiment commander and higher. Lower-ranking officers are not entitled to do that. A decision to place a soldier, a member of the military, before the disciplinary court is up to senior officers or direct superiors. So after the investigation which is phase one, the next phase is to take a decision that someone is going face disciplinary court. Only after that the disciplinary prosecutor can issue a bill of indictment. So we have a very strictly-prescribed procedure in these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just go back to my initial question. What happens with persons with regard to disciplinary proceedings whose service has been terminated?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: In such instances, if the disciplinary proceedings are still pending while the person is still member of the military, once his service is terminated, the proceedings are terminated as well, because the proceedings can only be conducted for as long as the perpetrator retains his status of professional serviceman. Once this status is terminated, the proceedings are also terminated and he could not be prosecuted any further, which is quite appropriate and natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Was there any possibility under the law for military disciplinary organ of the VJ to conduct disciplinary proceedings for violation of military discipline committed by a person serving in the Army of Republika Srpska or the Serbian Army of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: In order to consider disciplinary responsibility for any member of the army is something to be done by his superior officer. That means that no VJ officers had legal authority for that, and, therefore, he could not deliberate any instance of violation of military discipline on members of the Army of Republika Srpska or the Serbian Army of Krajina relating to his service in these two armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, are you aware that in the period following the break-up of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia there existed military judicial system in the Republic of Serbian Krajina and Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I know that both in the VRS and in the Army of the Serbian Republic of Krajina there existed military judiciary. Some of the judges of this court I knew personally, and with some of them I had some informal contacts during their term of office in their respective courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you tell us what kind of relationship was there between the military judiciary in Republika Srpska and the Serbian Republic of Krajina compared to the one that existed in the FRY?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The courts of the Yugoslav Army did not maintain any functional relationship with the above-mentioned courts. When I mentioned a minute ago that I personally knew some people from before because there were very few people working in military judiciary, these people remained there, but those were my private and personal contact that I had with them, and we occasionally consulted on some professional issues. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, can you please look at tab 5 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we please have in e-court D106.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, what kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: As I can see from the title itself, it is called guide-lines for determining the criteria for criminal prosecution, and on top we have the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and beneath the military prosecutor's office at the Main Staff of the army, and these guide-lines are indeed set out in a very professional and expert manner because I had an opportunity to go through them during proofing. This was not something that existed at the time. That was a novel approach because such guide-lines had not existed in the Yugoslav Army, either in terms of norms or factually, but since I had worked as a military prosecutor in Sarajevo, I know that guide-lines of this nature existed directing the work of the military prosecutor's office and were issued by the Commander-in-Chief at the time, that is Josip Bros Tito, who issued a similar document containing guide-lines for military prosecutors, but they mainly referred to the area of his responsibility provided under the law and other rules. Probably the people in the Main Staff of the VRS somehow came across these guide-lines because part of the military prosecutor archives had remained in Sarajevo and they used these old ones to write these new guide-lines in a rather fair and proper manner. According to these guide-lines, the prosecutor is, as the politicians would put it, encouraged to criminally prosecuted all members of the army who had committed certain crimes including those of International Humanitarian Law, so that gave sort of a carte blanche to the prosecutor stating that he would not be hindered in any way whatsoever in his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You already answered a number of questions that I had intended to ask you with regard to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now look at another document which is 65 ter Defence document 00001D.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, you should have this document that you can see on your screen now, you should have it in the binder as well. If I'm not wrong, that would be tab number 6.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, this is an order issued by the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I would kindly ask you to briefly comment on this document. Or let's be more efficient, I would like to point out to you a specific portion of this document, that is to say where this captain is sentenced to a disciplinary measure to serve a prison sentence?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you are asking me. This is indeed an order issued by the Sarajevo Corps or Romanija Corps pursuant to Article 79 of the Law on Army of Republika Srpska. The captain is sentenced to a prison term, as a disciplinary measure, of 20 days. This indicates that this law really provides for the possibility of an officer to send servicemen to prison for a disciplinary violation which had not been the case before because pursuant to basic constitutional principles, it was only a disciplinary court or regular court that could send someone to prison. Here we see that this was given as an exclusive right to an individual, an officer, and I would say that this was contrary to the constitution. Probably their constitution provided for this procedure, but if not, probably this was done due to practical reasons because the army was at the time involved in combat operations because this decision taken by the officer to imprison someone deviates from the basic principle of sentencing persons to prison only by courts. Here we have this as a discretionary right of an individual and this shows the difference between the norms that are applied here and the norms applicable in the law on the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, if I've understood you correctly, a disciplinary measure was -- well, not a disciplinary measure, a punishment, there's a difference in terminology there. So this type of punishment was not provided for disciplinary offences committed by the members of the Army of Yugoslavia. Could you explain that distinction to us.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I just indicated that according to the law governing the Army of Yugoslavia, a prison sentence of up to 20 days can be given but this is the military disciplinary court. That is the maximum sentence that disciplinary military courts can issue for disciplinary offences. But for a military officer, he cannot be give an prison sentence, a sentence of detention, military detention. It's only the military disciplinary court that can do that for disciplinary offences and that's a big difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document so that it be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Before we do, sir, I wonder if we could just scroll down a moment in the English version. I wonder, sir, if we could just get some clarification on who the signatory is to that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: General, can you recognise the signature? Who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: It says Commander Major-General Dragomir Milosevic. He was the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, so most probably that officer was given the legal possibility of issuing a disciplinary sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I note an error in the English translation it says Dragutin in English, whereas in the B/C/S version it is Dragomir, so my learned friend was quite right to ask the question because there's a difference in the two names in the two versions, the B/C/S and the English version. There's mistake in the English version. So not Dragutin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zorko. Yes, Mr. Thomas, are you happy?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: On that basis it can be admitted, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
